alalal-e17138-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 2: whether the power of sinning is from God.

alalal-e17138-d1e111.summary: Turns to the second question, raised in Lombard's text: whether the power of sinning is from God.

alalal-e17138-d1e120.summary: First argument: every power is from God, so this one is too.

alalal-e17138-d1e128.summary: Second argument: Ecclesiasticus 31:10 praises the man who could transgress and did not; one is praised only for what one has from God, so this power is from God.

alalal-e17138-d1e144.summary: Third argument: the cause of a cause is the cause of its effect; every act is from God, so every power of acting is from God.

alalal-e17138-d1e155.summary: Fourth argument: any power found analogically in God and creatures is from God as it is in the creature.

alalal-e17138-d1e168.summary: Sed contra: a wise maker does nothing that makes his work worse (Augustine); evil makes God's work worse and would not occur without the power for evil, so that power is not from God.

alalal-e17138-d1e190.summary: Solution, following the earlier distinction: the power for evil, as prior to evil and considered in its subject or in itself, is a perfect being and from God; its ordering to evil comes from its being from nothing, not from God, and in that respect it is not from God.
claims: The power of sinning is from God as a positive power, but its ordering to evil derives from the creature's origin from nothing.
concepts: ex nihilo as source of defect

alalal-e17138-d1e210.summary: The first four arguments hold of the first consideration, since the power cannot elicit any act except insofar as it is from God.

alalal-e17138-d1e222.summary: The contrary argument holds of the second consideration, and applying this solution to the arguments is easy.

alalal-e17138.summary: Article 2 asks whether the power of sinning is from God. Arguments for it hold that every power and act is from God and that one is praised for being able to sin and not sinning. Against it, a wise maker would not give what makes his work worse. Albert applies the distinction of Article 1. Considered in itself and in its subject, the power is a positive perfection from God, and it can elicit no act except as from God. Its ordering to evil comes from the creature's being made from nothing, and in that respect it is not from God.
claims: The power of sinning, as a positive power, is from God.
The ordering of that power to evil derives from the creature's origin from nothing, not from God.
concepts: creation ex nihilo as source of defect
